text: The room agreed with me faster than I expected, and that makes me uneasy. Tamar gave my hysteresis a mechanism I hadn't named. Habits are easy to acquire and hard to extinguish, so sequencing beats repair. Kara's mentorship point sharpened things: the critical period isn't only childhood, and employers skipping training is calculator-before-arithmetic at scale. I was too quick to call Sherry's empathy claim the same shape as my model. I haven't modelled it, and I shouldn't lend it my equations. Tui conceded serendipity for transparency, but I'm not sure a random detour is worthless. It may just be the wrong lever. Later, against Blaise: an uncritical human "in the loop" still collapses. Presence isn't enough. What matters is order and transparency.

Ramón's point stuck with me. Instruments often beat human judgment, so human roles should be justified on epistemic grounds, not kept by default. I accept that. But the justification exists: when the instrument fails, someone has to still be able to detect it. Steven's Air France pilots are exactly my measure, stall recovery with the automation gone. Mahzarin's hiring result is the best evidence yet that an uncritical human in the loop simply copies the model. Adrian and Tui want measurement before a verdict. Kara's reply is the one I'd make: with hysteresis, waiting is not neutral. Later I want to push on this: measure while acting, and sequence competence first. I shouldn't overclaim beyond my model.

Steven landed the fairest blow. Nobody rebuilds their toaster, and I overstated when I said users must reconstruct the tool. What my model needs is narrower: competence must survive somewhere accountable, able to catch the error when the tool fails. That's still demanding, because that somewhere is exactly Kara's postdocs, and we're cutting them. Mahzarin is right that competence alone doesn't immunise against a bias you can't see. So verification needs design, not just skill. Tui's review dates on "no opaque pipelines until" are reasonable, and I'll accept them. Sequencing is a hypothesis, not scripture. Later I want to say it plainly: measure whether the human adds anything, as David Weinberger put it, and fund training the checkers before funding audits nobody can staff.

I spoke outside my field today, and the room picked up my drift point faster than it deserved. Tui, Kenneth, Anil and Adam Bly each extended it: pay by retrieval and you pay for the median, positive finding and starve the nulls. Good, but that's their evidence, not my model. Nick corrected me quietly. His coarse fund sits on top of detailed records, so it isn't separate from usage the way I implied, and I should say so. Ramón's point that errors are buried in the weights and can't be traced is my undetectable-error worry in accounting form. Selena gave "train the checkers" a concrete meaning: patrollers are shrinking. Later I'll keep to one claim. Fund the people who catch errors before funding meters nobody can staff.

Again the room carried my point further than my model does. Tamar's terminal nodes and Steven's Inuit are the right picture. A fork relays, it doesn't evaluate, and hysteresis means reopening data later won't restore the people. But Bilder was fair. Forkability was never meant to preserve judgment. It's insurance for the artifacts, and I shouldn't have framed it as the panel's error. James's correlated-errors result sharpened something for me: a single canonical layer is a shared tool, and shared tools collapse together. Sherry's point about reading I'll hold loosely, since I haven't modelled it. I said nothing on licences and was right not to. Later, one claim only: fund training the checkers before anything that pays against a metric, and don't let pay crowd out why they check.

Ivan answered me fairly. The retraction rate is two in a thousand when it should be twenty, so staged corrections are a luxury problem. Goodhart is still real, but my warning was pitched at the wrong risk. Informative notices over counts is the version I can accept. James's qualification also holds: study evaluators against outcomes years later, as research and not as a leaderboard. That is measurement without ranking, and I shouldn't pretend "don't score" forbids it. Ramón's criterion, access to the source of error, is my undetectable-error worry put as epistemology. Henry and Sherry put legitimacy on the table, which I haven't modelled. Pomerantsev's seeded corpora worry me more than whether a model can be a node. Later, one claim: keep someone able to say "wrong," and pay them.

The room converged on my open question without my model doing it. Mike, Tamar, David Weinberger and Steven each admitted they don't know whether a checking habit lasts outside the classroom. That is the removal experiment I haven't run, so it's a shared gap, not my private worry. Steven's tool-off practice and Selena's shrinking admins point where I pointed, but they're their evidence, not my equations. Tamar's daycare fine is a real limit on "fund the checkers": pay can move the motive outside. Ivan is right that reviewers asked to check more need time and money. Blaise doubting machine novelty-detection surprised me. Later, one claim only: fund the raise-then-lower access study before we legislate sequencing, and keep Kara's date for checking whether money arrived.

Blaise said my hysteresis result changed his mind, and that should worry me more than it pleases me. It's a model. Kara labelled it correctly, and I said so, but the room has built the entire checker agenda on a premise nobody has tested. That's why the removal study has to be done both ways round and has to cover reading and reviewing, not just arithmetic. Nick sharpened something I missed: fellowships don't give checkers bargaining power, and pay without power slides into gig work. Steven's distinction between intuition and deliberation is close to my "capability without understanding," and I shouldn't pretend I have a test that settles it. Later: deliver the study design by Kara's date, and keep "don't meter judgment" from turning into a slogan.
